question_text: Solve cos x·dy/dx + y sin x = sec²x.

mark_split.label: Rewrite in standard form and identify P

insider_note: The equation must be divided by cos x before it matches the standard dy/dx + Py = Q form — skipping that division is the most common way students misidentify P and Q here.

steps.label: Rewrite in standard form and identify P
steps.margin_note: One mark. Divide the whole equation by cos x to reach the standard linear form.
steps.memory_tip: sin x/cos x = tan x and sec²x/cos x = sec³x — divide every term by cos x together.
lines: Given D.E is cos x·dy/dx + y sin x = sec²x
⇒ dy/dx + y(sin x/cos x) = sec²x/cos x
This is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x).
⇒ ∫P dx = ∫tan x dx = log sec x
steps.why: Dividing every term by cos x turns the coefficient of dy/dx into 1, which is required before the equation matches the standard linear form and P can be read off directly.
common_mistakes: Trying to identify P and Q before dividing by cos x, and reading P as sin x instead of tan x.
Simplifying sec²x/cos x incorrectly, forgetting it becomes sec³x.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e^(∫P dx) always.
steps.memory_tip: e^(log sec x) = sec x — the same simplification as every other linear equation with P = tan x.
lines: ∴ I.F. = e^(∫P dx) = e^(log sec x) = sec x
steps.why: Since P = tan x here just as in the two previous linear equations in this chapter, the integrating factor formula gives the same result: sec x.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to redo the I.F. calculation and copying a different integrating factor from a nearby question.
Writing I.F. as tan x instead of e raised to ∫P dx.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: Two marks. sec x · sec³x = sec⁴x, and sec⁴x splits into sec²x + sec²x·tan²x for integration.
steps.memory_tip: sec²x = 1 + tan²x — write sec⁴x = sec²x(1 + tan²x) so one piece integrates plainly and the other by a direct substitution.
lines: Hence the solution is y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx
⇒ y sec x = ∫sec x·sec³x dx = ∫sec⁴x dx

lines.text: y sec x = tan x + tan³x/3 + c

steps.why: Writing sec⁴x as sec²x(1 + tan²x) splits it into a plain sec²x integral and a sec²x·tan²x term, and since sec²x is the derivative of tan x, the second piece integrates directly using tan x as the new variable.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate sec⁴x directly without the sec²x = 1 + tan²x identity.
Missing the /3 that comes from integrating tan²x·sec²x, which uses the power rule on tan x.
